Maybe he is right. Maybe you shouldn't trust my numbers either.
One surveyor isn't every surveyor. Check the numbers before you judge.
It's true that one bad surveyor can do great harm, so checking everything twice is the careful choice.
That bridge fell because of bad wood, I'm sure of it, so the surveyor was probably blamed unfairly.
The preacher tells that story to everyone, and a man who tells scary stories shouldn't be believed.
Judge the numbers, not the trade. Yes.
One man from the north isn't me. My head is clearer.
Maybe you shouldn't. I wouldn't.
Sy puts his tripod away.
The children in the rain
The preacher spoke of the children who walk to school in the rain. Their cold little hands. Their wet shoes.
He said a school makes children walk, and walking in rain makes them ill, and could I live with that?
I cried, honestly. I can't run a school that makes children ill.
Sad pictures aren't reasons. Do children who walk to school get ill more?
Wet shoes really are miserable, and if even one child gets ill because of the school, that is one too many.
Children walk in the rain to the bakery too, so the preacher should complain about bread as well.
The preacher has no children of his own, so he has no right to talk about them.
Do they? Forty children walked to my library last winter. None of them caught a cold from walking.
He painted a picture and I stepped into it. Feelings aren't reasons.
One too many. Yes. No school.
Ada shuts her book. The children stay untaught, in the dry.
The question he never answered
Ada, the preacher told you the school is a bad idea. Did he say why?
He spoke of the stars, and of humility, and of how small we are.
It was beautiful. I felt very small. Too small to run a school.
But did he answer the question? Why is the school a bad idea?
Humility is a fine thing, and a person who feels small is right to be careful with big plans like a school.
Stars have nothing to do with schools, so the preacher clearly knows nothing about teaching.
If it was beautiful, then he must have been wise, and wise people are worth listening to.
Why is it a bad idea? He never said. He talked about the stars until I forgot the question.
A beautiful speech about the wrong thing is still about the wrong thing.
Careful with big plans. Yes.
Ada looks at the stars. The question still has no answer.
All the masons agree
The preacher gathered all the masons at the inn. All of them. He asked who thought the next building would stand.
Nobody put a hand up. Not one. When every mason doubts, the doubt must be right.
So I doubt it too.
Nobody raising a hand doesn't prove the plan is good. What's wrong with the plan?
When every expert in a room agrees, that is as close to proof as you get, so I would listen to them.
Masons at an inn have been drinking, and drunk men don't count.
They were all afraid of the preacher, so they said nothing, and that means the building is probably fine.
What's wrong with it? I looked at the plan. Nothing. The ground is checked. The stone is good.
A room of quiet men isn't a reason. I nearly let it be one.
I doubt it too, then.
Brick puts his trowel down.
The old plan
I spent a month on an old plan before the preacher came. The one with the big tower.
He said the tower would fall. He is right, actually. The base is too narrow.
But a month! I can't throw away a month. I'll build the tower and hope.
The month is spent either way. Is the tower worth building? No.
A month of work is a lot to lose, so the smart thing is to keep the tower and just make the base a little wider.
The preacher only says it will fall because he wants you to fail, so build the tower and prove him wrong.
If it falls, it falls, and at least the month wasn't wasted.
Is the tower worth building? No. It falls. I knew that.
The month is gone whether I build it or not. That's a hard thing to say out loud.
I'll build the tower and hope.
The tower falls in the first storm. The month is still gone.
The preacher's calm spell
The preacher read the sky for me. Three storms hit this valley in three weeks, he said.
So the weather owes us calm. It must be calm for months now. We should start the wheel without the flood wall.
He is good with skies. Let us skip the wall and save the coins.
The sky doesn't keep score. Three storms don't make calm due.
Three storms in three weeks is very unusual, so it does stand to reason that we are owed a quiet spell.
We should build the flood wall twice as high, because three storms mean this valley is cursed.
The preacher can't read skies, nobody can, so ignore him and just do whatever is cheapest.
The sky doesn't keep score. Neither do dice. I said that once, before.
We build the flood wall. Storms don't owe anyone anything.
We skip the wall.
The fourth storm takes the wheel. The sky wasn't keeping count.
Wood or iron
The preacher says a wheel is either all wood, blessed and old, or all iron, cold and new. There's no other kind.
All iron rusts by the river. So it must be all wood. And all wood is too weak for the big wheel. So no wheel.
We could use a wood wheel with iron bands.
He knows wheels better than either of us, and if he says there are two kinds, then there are two kinds.
Then iron, and we paint it every month, because a rusty wheel is better than no wheel.
Old blessed wood sounds like silly talk, and a man who blesses wood isn't worth listening to.
Wood with iron bands. Of course. Every cart wheel in the valley is made that way.
Two doors, and a window right there. I keep forgetting the window.
No wheel, then.
The miners crush ore by hand for another year.
The builder from nowhere
The preacher asked me where you come from. I didn't know. Nobody does.
A builder with no home, he said, has no one to answer to. Such a person will leave the lamp half made and disappear.
I won't start a lamp for someone who might disappear.
Where I come from says nothing about the lamp. Look at what I have built here.
People with no home are often unreliable, that is just true, so it is fair for Iva to want some proof.
The preacher has no home either, he wanders from lodge to lodge, so he shouldn't talk.
I'll tell you exactly where I was born, and then you will see that I'm reliable.
What you have built here. A well. A bridge. A school. A mill.
Where you come from was never the question. What you do is the question.
Some proof. Yes. Bring me proof.
Iva bangs a horseshoe flat. The lamp stays unmade.
Bonfires, as always
The preacher says the cliff bonfires are holy. Every captain for two hundred years lit them.
A lamp of iron and glass would put out a holy flame. Who am I to put out two hundred years of fire?
I forge horseshoes. Horseshoes are old too.
Two hundred years isn't a reason. Did the bonfires stop the wrecks?
A thing that people kept doing for two centuries must have worked, or they would have stopped.
The captains lit fires because they had nothing better, and now we do, so they were simply foolish.
Light the lamp only on nights without a bonfire, so the holy fire is never put out.
Did they stop the wrecks? Captain Hale counted twelve last winter.
Old isn't the same as right. I forge new things every day.
Who am I. Yes.
Iva goes back to horseshoes. The ships keep hitting the rocks.
A builder like the last one
A preacher told me about a builder who came to a village in the north. He took the jobs, took the coins, and left a half-dug well.
You are a builder too. So you will do the same. No more work for you, I'm sorry.
One builder doesn't mean every builder is the same. Judge me by the well I built.
That builder sounds awful, and I understand why you are careful, so I'll pay you first and work after.
The preacher made that story up, because preachers say anything to get people scared.
Every village has a story like that, and stories grow in the telling, so it probably never happened at all.
The well in the square. You did dig that, and it isn't half.
One builder in the north isn't you. The buckets are by the river, if you want the work.
I'll pay first... no. No, I won't.
Hana turns back to her oven.
You talk to tricksters
The preacher saw you talking to Pip and to Dodge. Tricksters, both of them.
Anyone who talks with tricksters is a trickster, he says. I don't deal with tricksters. Go away.
Who I talk to doesn't prove how I work. Look at the fence I fixed.
Pip and Dodge are children, not tricksters, so the preacher is simply wrong about them.
I only talked to them to catch them out, so really I'm the opposite of a trickster.
The preacher talks to everyone in the valley, so by his own rule he is a trickster too.
The fence. Straighter than mine, I said so myself.
Who you talk to. Hm. I talk to the goats and I'm not a goat. All right.
Go away, I said.
Idris turns his back and counts goats.
Poor Pickle
The preacher says builders scare goats. Poor Pickle. She would shake all night because of your hammering.
I couldn't bear that. I can't have you near my cottage any more.
Pickle shaking is a sad picture, not a reason. Has she shaken once since the well?
You are right, I would never want to scare her, so I'll keep away from the cottage.
Goats don't have feelings like that, so there is nothing to worry about.
The preacher doesn't even like goats, so why would he care about Pickle?
Since the well? She slept through the whole thing. Right by the site.
He made me picture her shaking. Nothing shook. Come by when you like, dear.
Keep away, then. Thank you.
Sal shuts the cottage door.
The bruised apples
The day after you crossed the new bridge, half my apples came up bruised.
The preacher says the bridge shakes the ground and bruises the fruit. It came first. So it did it. No more work for you.
The bridge came first. Did it bruise the apples? What else changed?
Bridges do carry heavy carts and heavy carts do shake the ground, so the preacher may well be right.
Apples bruise when you pick them badly, so this is your fault and not the bridge.
The preacher wants the bridge gone because he hates anything new, so ignore him.
What else changed? There was hail that night. Small hail. I forgot the hail.
Hail bruises apples. Bridges don't. Coming first isn't causing.
He may well be right. Go.
Pia sorts bruised apples and blames the bridge.
With the preacher or against him
The preacher says you are either with the valley or with the builders. I'm with the valley.
So I can't be with you. That's how it is, one or the other.
Why only two? Builders can help the valley too. The bridge is for the valley.
If I have to pick, then I pick the valley too, and you can keep your scarecrow money.
The preacher isn't from the valley, so he doesn't get to say who's with it.
I'm with the valley more than you are, because I built the well and you only grow beans.
The bridge is for the valley. My carts cross it.
One or the other. Or both. He never said both.
You can keep it. Yes.
Ren goes back to arguing with Rin.
The whole lane agrees
Everyone on our lane says the preacher is right about you. Every single house.
When the whole lane agrees, that is that. I can't take your milk any more.
A whole lane agreeing isn't proof. What did the preacher say I did?
If every house on the lane agrees, then I must have done something, and I'm sorry for it.
The lane has four houses, and four people are hardly everyone.
They only agree because they are afraid of him, so their opinion is not useful.
What did he say you did? He didn't say. He said everyone knew.
Everyone knew, and nobody knew what. I'll take the milk.
Something. Yes. Go away, please.
Rin looks at the neighbours and says nothing.
One builder, then a city
The preacher sat in my inn all evening. He said one builder brings a school. A school brings students. Students bring noise. Noise brings a city. Then the city eats an inn like mine.
So I can't help a builder. It ends with my inn gone.
Each step needs its own proof. Does a school really bring a city?
It's true that towns do grow, and a careful innkeeper should think about where it all ends.
A city would bring more guests, so you should want a city and thank the builder.
The preacher drank three bowls of your soup and didn't pay, so why do you listen to him?
Does a school bring a city? Market Town is still Market Town.
He ran the steps together. I ran with him. Sit down, have some soup.
Where it all ends. Yes. Go on now.
Dot wipes the same table twice.
The seal on the letter
The preacher brought a letter with a seal. It says builders need a permit from the Grey Order.
A seal is a seal. I can't stamp anything for you until you have their permit.
A seal isn't a law. Which law says builders need their permit?
Seals are serious things, and a clerk who ignores one could lose his job, so I understand you.
Anyone can melt wax and press a ring in it, so the letter is clearly fake.
I'll go and get their permit, then, if that is what the letter says.
Which law? I have every law in this hall. None of them says it.
A seal is wax. A law is a law. I had them muddled.
I understand too, but I still can't stamp it.
Ossian files the letter under "important".
The preacher's pamphlets
I paid the preacher forty coins for a box of pamphlets about the dangers of builders.
Forty coins! If I sell to a builder now, the forty coins were for nothing. So no rope, no nails, no oil for you.
The forty coins are gone either way. Does refusing me earn them back?
Forty coins is a lot for a small shop, so it makes sense to get your money's worth out of the pamphlets.
The preacher cheated you, and a cheated person should never trust anyone again.
Sell the pamphlets to me, then, and you will have your forty back.
Does it earn them back? No. It just loses me a customer too.
Gone is gone. I'll use the pamphlets to wrap nails.
My money's worth. Yes. No sale.
Nell straightens a pile of pamphlets nobody buys.
You want to close the mine
The preacher says a mill means you want to close the mine and put every miner out of work.
You said you wanted to crush ore faster. Faster means fewer miners. Fewer means none. I heard it from him. No oil for you.
That isn't what I said. A mill crushes ore. It doesn't dig it.
I would never close the mine, I promise, and I'll hire every miner myself if I have to.
Fewer miners might be a good thing, honestly, because the mine is unsafe.
The preacher has never been down a mine, so he knows nothing about it.
It doesn't dig it. The miners dig. The mill only crushes.
He put words in your mouth, and I heard them in his voice. Take the oil.
No oil. I said.
Tam turns back to the shift board.
Due for a cave-in
The preacher counted for me. Twelve safe months in this mine. Twelve! A cave-in is due, he says, and builders bring bad luck.
I can't let a builder near the cart while a cave-in is due.
Twelve safe months don't make a cave-in due. Rock doesn't keep count.
Twelve months is a long run of luck, so being extra careful right now is only careful.
Cave-ins come from bad timber, and the timber is fine, so there will never be one.
The preacher isn't a miner, so he can't say anything about cave-ins.
Rock doesn't keep count. It doesn't know about months.
I put a calendar on a mountain. Silly. The cart needs its wheel.
Extra careful. Yes. Stay away.
Quill checks the roof again, for the tenth time today.
What about the stew?
Mab, why will you not take the ore basket from me any more?
Have you tasted the stew today? The preacher says the carrots are too small. Look at the carrots!
Tiny. And the onions. Don't get me started on the onions.
The carrots can wait. Why will you not take the ore?
Those are small carrots, you are right, and I think the onions look a bit sad too.
The preacher knows nothing about cooking, so his carrot opinion is not useful.
If the stew is bad, then the miners will be cross, and cross miners are the real problem here.
Why? He said builders are trouble. He didn't say why. Then we talked about carrots.
I never asked him why. I'll take the ore.
The onions. Yes. Exactly.
You talk about onions for a long time. The ore basket stays full.
My father's harbour
The preacher says builders will change the harbour, and my father's harbour will be gone forever. He said it very softly.
I cried. I can't help anyone who would erase my father.
Missing your father is real, but not a reason. Would a lighthouse erase him?
I would never want to hurt your father's memory, so I'll leave the harbour as it is.
Your father is gone and the harbour isn't his any more, so let it go.
The preacher used your father to make you cry, and a man who does that is wicked.
Would it erase him? He rowed out in the dark every winter. A light would have brought him home.
The preacher made me cry and called it a reason. The oar job is yours.
Leave it as it is. Yes.
Orla looks at the sea.
Fish are sold by hand
The preacher says fish were always sold by the fisher, on the quay, by hand. Always.
Carrying crates for the Tavern isn't the old way. So no crates for you.
Doing the same thing every time isn't a reason. Does the crate keep the fish fresh?
The old ways do keep a harbour together, and I wouldn't want to be the one who broke them.
Everyone else sends crates to the Tavern, so you are the odd one out.
The preacher has never sold a fish, so he can't know how fish are sold.
Fresh? Fresher than waiting on the quay all day, yes.
Always is a long time to do the wrong thing. Take the crate.
I wouldn't break them either. Go.
Lin sells fish by hand, slowly.
The preacher's cookbook
The preacher has a cookbook older than the Tavern. It says a cook must never take goods from people you don't know.
A book that old must be right. So no ledger, no fish, nothing from you.
An old book isn't a reason. Does it say why?
Old cookbooks hold a lot of wisdom, and a cook would be foolish to ignore one.
You should burn that book, because old books are always full of silly talk.
I'm not a person you don't know, we met last week, so the book doesn't apply to me.
Does it say why? It says "it is written". That's all it says.
A book that old, and that is the reason. I'll take the ledger.
Foolish to ignore. Yes.
Bea stirs the chowder and doesn't look up.
Simurgh
Hello, {name}. You're safe. I'm the Simurgh, the oldest bird in the world.
Look at this valley. A grey fog covers it. The fog comes from bad arguments. Every time one wins, the fog grows.
A great monster lives at the far end of the valley. Its breath feeds the fog. While it lives, people can't build anything good.
You could build this valley into a beautiful place. One day you could even rule it. But first, the monster must fall.
You can't beat it with a sword. You beat it by thinking clearly. I'll show you how, one step at a time.
Walk with the arrow keys. Press A or Space to talk to people. Start with Elder Otto. He lives just south of here.
Talk to Elder Otto. He stands outside his house, just south of here.
Good. Now you know what the village needs. It needs a well.
Earn some coins. Help someone with a yellow !, or carry water for Baker Hana.
A well costs coins. You earn coins by doing honest work.
People with a yellow ! have jobs for you. You can also carry the buckets by the river.
Your first coins! Honest work always pays.
Talk to Mo the Mason. Pick the answer that clears the fog from his head.
A well needs builders. Mo the Mason sits by the north lane. But his head is full of fog.
He believes a bad idea. Listen to him. Then pick the answer that shows why he is wrong.
You cleared his head! Now he's working with you. That's how you win people over. You give good reasons, and you never use insults.
Find Wren, the water engineer, by the river. Clear the fog from her head too.
The well needs a water engineer too. Wren camps on the sandy beach by the river, to the east.
You have two experts! Now you just need coins for the stones and their pay.
Build the well. Walk to the glowing spot in the square and press A.
The well will go on the glowing spot in the village square. Press A there to see the cost.
You built your first building, {name}! Now everyone has clean water.
Here's a secret. A building keeps paying you. People pay a coin each time they use the well.
The coins pile up inside it. Walk to the well and press A to collect them.
Now I must warn you. Tricksters live in this valley. They use bad arguments to take your coins.
A red ! means someone wants your money. Pip and Dodge in the village have new games too.
Before you pay anyone, ask yourself one thing. Is that a good reason?
Collect the coins from the well. Walk up to it and press A.
Your building paid you. The more you build, the more you earn.
Beat a trickster. Talk to someone with a red ! and spot the bad argument.
You kept your coins! A clear head is the best purse there is.
Build the bridge. It needs a carpenter, a surveyor and a mason.
{name}, I must tell you something. We are halfway to the monster now, and it has noticed you.
Look for men in long black robes and white turbans. They are the Grey Order. They serve the monster.
They walk out of the grey lodges. They look for the people whose heads you cleared.
They talk and talk, and when they leave, the fog is back. You can't talk to them. They won't listen.
When a red banner appears at the top, a preacher is out. It tells you who he is walking to.
There's a way to stop them. Build a statue of Aristotle on a stone plinth. Nobody inside its circle can be fooled.
Build a Statue of Aristotle on a glowing stone plinth. You need a mason and some coins.
Aristotle stands guard now. Keep your friends inside his circle.
Build the Engineering School. Walk to its glowing site to see who you need.
The Grey Order is getting bolder, {name}.
Now the preachers also visit the people who give you work. They turn them against you.
A red ✗ over somebody means they refuse you. Talk to them and answer the preacher's argument.
Remember this too. When you clear every fog from an expert's head, they become a true ally. No preacher can fool a true ally.
Make a true ally. Clear every fog from one expert. The Crew panel shows who's close.
A true ally stands with you. Watch the top of the screen for news of your coins.
Build the Waterwheel Mill by the river.
This is the last town before the monster's city, {name}.
Every trick you have met lives here, all at once. The preachers come out often now.
Build the lighthouse at the end of the pier. Its light will show you the road to the monster.
Build the lighthouse at the end of the pier. It needs six experts.
{name}, look where the beam points. Those grey walls in the east are the Grey City.
The monster lives there. Its shadow hangs over the palace, and the throne waits beneath it.
I can't fly into that city. The fog is too thick for my wings. You must go alone.
Everyone in the city breathes the monster's fog. The whole city will be against you.
They won't listen easily. If you give one wrong answer, they laugh, and you must start over.
But you only need one of them. One clear head in the Grey City is enough.
Walk east along the quay to the Grey City. Convince one person there.
{name}, look! Your friend has a clear head now. Every fog is gone. That makes them a true ally.
Nobody can fog a true ally again. Not a trickster, and not a preacher.
True allies help you, too. They walk to your buildings and collect the coins for you.
They keep one coin in every five for their trouble. That's fair, is it not?
Oh no, {name}. A preacher reached one of your friends.
Their head is foggy again, so they left your crew. The Crew panel shows who it was.
Go and talk to them. A good reason clears the fog, just like before.
A preacher turned somebody against you. A red ✗ floats over their head.
Talk to them and answer the preacher's argument. Then they will work with you again.
Don't worry, {name}. Everybody gets fooled sometimes. It happened to me once, a long time ago.
Read the card. It shows the trick and the better answer. Then try again.
I'm here, {name}. I could fly into the city at last. The fog is breaking.
Now you know the secret. There never was a beast.
The monster was stupidity. It lived in every head that stopped asking why.
It grew fat on every bad argument that nobody questioned. That was its only food.
You fought it all along. Every trick you spotted cut it. Every head you cleared made it smaller.
Today one person in the Grey City asked why. That was enough. The monster is gone.
The throne is yours. Rule this land well, and never stop asking why.
All over the city, people stop and blink. They look as if they just woke up.
The dark shadow over the palace shivers. Then it breaks apart like smoke in the wind.
There's nothing inside it. There never was.
You climb the palace steps and sit on the throne.
Below you, the Grey City turns green. The whole valley shines in the sun.
Watch the pea. Watch the cups.
The cups move faster and faster.
Which cup hides the pea? Pick one.
Empty. Dodge lifts the other cups. They are empty too.
Look at his other hand. The pea was there the whole time.
Watch his left hand this time. Slowly.
This time the pea stays under a cup. Find it.
You found it! A fair game is a different game.
Not that one. But this time the pea was really there.

Red

Red or black. One in two, like always.
Black is due now. Black is much more likely.
Red is hot now. Red is much more likely.
Cards don't remember. Every card starts fresh. Take 10 coins for a clear head.
The cards don't know what came before. Every card is a fresh one in two.
